# Aṅguttara-Nikāya. XI.

Just as, venerable sir, a <term>rajoharaṇaṃ</term> <gloss>dust-cloth or rag</gloss> wipes up what is clean and wipes up what is unclean, wipes up what is smeared with excrement, wipes up what is smeared with urine, wipes up what is smeared with saliva, wipes up what is smeared with pus, and wipes up what is smeared with blood, yet the dust-cloth is not annoyed or disgusted by it: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like a dust-cloth, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Truly, venerable sir, only one who does not have <term>kāyagatā sati</term> <gloss>mindfulness directed to the body</gloss> established in the body might strike a fellow monk here and, without apologizing, depart on a journey.

Just as, venerable sir, an <term>caṇḍālakumārako</term> <gloss>outcast boy</gloss> or an <term>caṇḍālakumārikā</term> <gloss>outcast girl</gloss>, basket in hand, wearing rags, when entering a village or a town, enters with a truly humble mind: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like an outcast boy, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Truly, venerable sir, only one who does not have mindfulness directed to the body established in the body might strike a fellow monk here and, without apologizing, depart on a journey.

Just as, venerable sir, a <term>usabho chinnavisāṇo</term> <gloss>bull with its horns cut off</gloss>, gentle, well-tamed, and well-disciplined, when wandering from street to street and square to square, does not hurt anyone with its foot or its horn: even so, venerable sir, do I dwell with a mind like a bull with its horns cut off, vast, exalted, measureless, without enmity, and without ill-will. Truly, venerable sir, only one who does not have mindfulness directed to the body established in the body might strike a fellow monk here and, without apologizing, depart on a journey.

Just as, venerable sir, a woman or a man, young, youthful, fond of ornaments, having bathed their head, [would be disgusted] by a snake's carcass or...

---

<note>
¹ Manuscript variants: In the Thai and Burmese M6 and M editions, the word is "puñjati"; the Sinhalese edition uses "muñcati" throughout.
² This phrase is omitted by the Burmese M, Ph, Thai, and Sinhalese manuscripts.
³ This phrase is omitted by the Burmese M, Ph, and Sinhalese manuscripts.
⁴ This phrase is omitted by the Burmese M, Ph, M6, and Sinhalese manuscripts.
⁵ This phrase is omitted by the Thai manuscript.
⁶ This phrase is omitted by the Burmese M, Ph, M6, and Sinhalese manuscripts.
⁷ The Burmese M6 and M editions abbreviate the text here until the word "striking" (āsajja).
⁸ The Thai manuscript reads "kumāro" (youth/prince).
⁹ The Thai manuscript reads "kumārī" (maiden/princess).
¹⁰ The Ph manuscript reads "kaḷoviº".
¹¹ The Burmese M6 manuscript reads "nantakaº"; the Thai and Burmese M6 and M manuscripts read "vāsini".
¹² The Burmese M manuscript reads "caṇḍālakumārakacaṇḍālakumārikaº".
¹³ The Burmese M and Sinhalese manuscripts read "surato".
¹⁴ The Sinhalese manuscript reads "sikkhito" (well-trained).
¹⁵ The Thai and Burmese M6 and M manuscripts read "rathiyā".
¹⁶ This phrase is omitted by the Burmese M and Ph manuscripts.
¹⁷ The Thai manuscript reads "maṇḍanaº".
¹⁸ This phrase is omitted by the Sinhalese manuscript.
</note>

<summary>Venerable Sariputta defends his conduct through a series of analogies, comparing his humble and non-reactive state of mind to a dust-cloth, an outcast youth, and a bull with its horns removed. These metaphors illustrate the quality of a mind perfected through mindfulness of the body and lack of ill-will toward others.</summary>

<keywords>Sariputta, humility, mindfulness of the body, Buddhist similes, non-violence, Aṅguttara Nikāya, monastic discipline</keywords>
